_Comment: Metadata for snipSettings.ini (ScreenSnip).  Every key carries restart:..\ScreenSnip.exe because settings are read once at load: the SnipCfg() loader caches the whole INI on first read, and the add-on modules' class statics initialise before the auto-execute section.  NOTE: a restart closes all open snips.  Keys typed 'text' with a decimal validation regex are FLOATS awaiting a float type in SettingsManager; their intended ranges are stated in the help text.

Capture.SelectionColor.label: SelectionColor
Capture.SelectionColor.help:
color of the semi-transparent overlay drawn while you drag out a selection.

Six hex digits, RRGGBB, with no 0x or # prefix.

BorderColor is set to this same value by default so the selection tint and the finished snip's frame read as one UI. If you change one and want them to keep matching, change both.

Capture.SelectionOverlayAlpha.label: SelectionOverlayAlpha
Capture.SelectionOverlayAlpha.help:
Opacity of the selection overlay: 0 is invisible, 255 is solid.

80 is light enough to see the content you are framing through the tint. Raise it if the overlay is hard to spot against busy screens; lower it if it obscures what you are trying to select.

Capture.CaptureAdjustMargin.label: CaptureAdjustMargin
Capture.CaptureAdjustMargin.help:
Extra pixels captured AROUND your selection into a frozen 'master' snapshot, so the capture region can be nudged, panned and resized after the fact (see the ADJUST CAPTURE REGION hotkeys). This is the maximum you can pan or grow in any direction before hitting the edge of the snapshot.

Larger means more adjustment headroom but more memory per snip - a 32-bit bitmap costs width x height x 4 bytes.

0 = no headroom; the region is fixed at the exact selection.
150 = comfortable for fixing small clipped edges.
99999 = effectively snapshots the WHOLE desktop into every snip.

The value is always clamped to the virtual desktop bounds, so oversized numbers are safe - they just capture everything and use more RAM. They will not crash or read off-screen.

This margin is also what supplies the extra pixels a Straighten pulls in, so a larger margin allows a larger clean deskew before the corners run past the snapshot edge.

DimensionLabels.ShowDimensionLabels.label: ShowDimensionLabels
DimensionLabels.ShowDimensionLabels.help:
Master switch for the on-screen width and height readouts.

Disabling turns off BOTH the capture-time labels (shown while Ctrl+RButton dragging) and the post-capture resize labels (shown while Alt-dragging a snip's edge).

DimensionLabels.InfoFontSize.label: InfoFontSize
DimensionLabels.InfoFontSize.help:
Font size in points for the W and H dimension labels shown during a selection.

The labels are drawn in bold Courier New so the digits stay a fixed width and do not jitter as the numbers change.

DimensionLabels.InfoWHOffsetRight.label: InfoWHOffsetRight
DimensionLabels.InfoWHOffsetRight.help:
Inset in pixels from the right edge of the selection for the H (height) label.

Increase to pull the label further inside the selection rectangle.

DimensionLabels.InfoWHOffsetBottom.label: InfoWHOffsetBottom
DimensionLabels.InfoWHOffsetBottom.help:
Inset in pixels from the bottom edge of the selection for the W (width) label.

Increase to pull the label further inside the selection rectangle.

DimensionLabels.InfoWMinWidth.label: InfoWMinWidth
DimensionLabels.InfoWMinWidth.help:
The selection must be at least this many pixels WIDE before the W label appears.

Stops the label from overflowing a selection too small to hold it.

DimensionLabels.InfoHMinHeight.label: InfoHMinHeight
DimensionLabels.InfoHMinHeight.help:
The selection must be at least this many pixels TALL before the H label appears.

Stops the label from overflowing a selection too small to hold it.

FreezeCapture.FreezeCaptureKey.label: FreezeCaptureKey
FreezeCapture.FreezeCaptureKey.help:
Key that triggers Freeze Capture. Any single key AHK understands: ScrollLock, PrintScreen, CapsLock, Pause, F12, and so on. Set to blank to disable the built-in trigger entirely - the cross-script message trigger still works.

Why Freeze Capture exists: a normal Ctrl+RButton drag cannot capture a context menu, tooltip or drop-down, because pressing a mouse button dismisses them. A KEYBOARD trigger fixes that. The instant you press it the entire virtual desktop is copied into memory and a full-screen backdrop showing that frozen image goes up, so the real menu is free to close - its pixels are already captured.

Choosing a key:
ScrollLock - almost nothing else uses it, it has a status LED, and no app fights you for it.
PrintScreen - the conventional choice, BUT SnagIt and Windows 11's Snipping Tool both grab it.
CapsLock - fine IF no other script already claims CapsLock. Each AHK script installs its own keyboard hook, and a consuming CapsLock hotkey in an earlier hook means this one never sees the key.

If another script already owns the key you want, let it keep the key and have it broadcast the AHK_ScreenSnip_FreezeCapture window message instead. See the cross-script trigger comment in ScreenSnip.ahk.

FreezeCapture.FreezeDoublePress.label: FreezeDoublePress
FreezeCapture.FreezeDoublePress.help:
Require a DOUBLE press of FreezeCaptureKey, or fire on a single press?

Double-press is recommended for keys that have a normal function or a toggle state. The hotkey is registered with '~' (pass-through), so two presses of a toggle key like CapsLock or ScrollLock turn it on and then straight back off, leaving the lock state exactly as it was.

FreezeCapture.FreezeDoublePressTime.label: FreezeDoublePressTime
FreezeCapture.FreezeDoublePressTime.help:
Maximum gap in milliseconds between the two presses when FreezeDoublePress is on.

Too short and the double-tap is hard to land; too long and a pair of unrelated presses can trigger a capture by accident.

FreezeCapture.FreezeNullifyCapsLock.label: FreezeNullifyCapsLock
FreezeCapture.FreezeNullifyCapsLock.help:
Nullify a CapsLock SINGLE press while ScreenSnip is running?

This only has any effect when FreezeCaptureKey is CapsLock. It is ignored for every other key, so it cannot surprise someone who never chose CapsLock.

Why it exists: the trigger is registered with '~' (pass-through), so a DOUBLE press toggles CapsLock on and then straight back off and nets out. A single stray press has nothing to cancel it and leaves CapsLock on. If you are one of the many people who never use CapsLock deliberately, switch this on and ScreenSnip will turn it back off after every press, single or double.

This does NOT block other scripts. The hotkey is non-suppressing, so any other app's CapsLock binding still fires - only the LOCK STATE is reset afterwards. If another script USES the caps state rather than just hotkeying on the key, leave this off.

The shipped ScreenSnip default is off, on the grounds that turning a key off on someone's keyboard is not a decision an app should make for them.

FreezeHint.ShowFreezeHint.label: ShowFreezeHint
FreezeHint.ShowFreezeHint.help:
Show the hint message over the frozen backdrop during a Freeze Capture?

Turn it off for a silently frozen screen - only worth doing once the gesture is deep muscle memory, since a frozen screen with no explanation is alarming.

The hint floats ABOVE the frozen image and is never included in the snip, so it costs you nothing in the capture.

FreezeHint.FreezeHintText.label: FreezeHintText
FreezeHint.FreezeHintText.help:
Hint message shown over the frozen backdrop.

Use `n (backtick n) for a line break.

Because the crop reads from the frozen bitmap rather than the screen, this text is invisible to the capture by construction - so it can be large and central without obscuring anything.

This version is used when SnipWinDetect.ahk is ABSENT. When that module is present, FreezeHintTextWinDetect is shown instead.
FreezeHint.FreezeHintText.default: ScreenSnip has frozen the screen.`nRight-click-drag to select a region.`n`nThe new snip will "float" above the screen.`n`nEsc cancels.

FreezeHint.FreezeHintTextWinDetect.label: FreezeHintTextWinDetect
FreezeHint.FreezeHintTextWinDetect.help:
Hint message shown INSTEAD of FreezeHintText when SnipWinDetect.ahk is present, because the gesture set is genuinely different then - a left-click grabs a whole highlighted window.

Use `n (backtick n) for a line break.

Kept as a separate string rather than a line appended to the other one so that deleting the module leaves the hint truthful. Otherwise it would advertise a click that does nothing.
FreezeHint.FreezeHintTextWinDetect.default: ScreenSnip has frozen the screen.`nLeft-click a highlighted window to grab it whole,`nor right-click-drag to select any region.`n`nThe new snip will "float" above the screen.`n`nEsc cancels.

FreezeHint.FreezeHintFontName.label: FreezeHintFontName
FreezeHint.FreezeHintFontName.help: Font family for the freeze hint pill. Any installed font name.

FreezeHint.FreezeHintFontSize.label: FreezeHintFontSize
FreezeHint.FreezeHintFontSize.help:
Point size for the freeze hint text.

The hint sits above the frozen image and never appears in the capture, so it can be generously large without any cost to the snip.

FreezeHint.FreezeHintTextColor.label: FreezeHintTextColor
FreezeHint.FreezeHintTextColor.help:
Text color of the freeze hint pill, six hex digits RRGGBB with no 0x prefix.

TipTextColor is set to this same value by default so the hint and the status tooltips read as one UI.

FreezeHint.FreezeHintBackColor.label: FreezeHintBackColor
FreezeHint.FreezeHintBackColor.help:
Background color of the freeze hint pill, six hex digits RRGGBB with no 0x prefix.

TipBackColor is set to this same value by default so the hint and the status tooltips read as one UI.

FreezeHint.FreezeHintAlpha.label: FreezeHintAlpha
FreezeHint.FreezeHintAlpha.help:
Overall opacity of the hint pill: 0 is invisible, 255 is solid.

Deliberately semi-transparent so anything directly underneath it is still readable while you aim the selection.

FreezeHint.FreezeHintCornerRadius.label: FreezeHintCornerRadius
FreezeHint.FreezeHintCornerRadius.help: Corner rounding of the hint pill, in pixels. 0 gives square corners.

SnipWindow.ShowSnipBorder.label: ShowSnipBorder
SnipWindow.ShowSnipBorder.help:
Show a coloured border around each floating snip?

Off gives a fully borderless, image-only snip.

Note that the border is suppressed during rotations other than 0, 90, 180 and 270 degrees, because a rectangular frame does not map cleanly onto a tilted snip.

SnipWindow.BorderColor.label: BorderColor
SnipWindow.BorderColor.help:
Border color for floating snips, six hex digits RRGGBB with no 0x prefix.

Shipped matching SelectionColor so the selection overlay and the finished snip feel cohesive. Override it to any color you like - if you want the two to keep matching, change both.

SnipWindow.BorderThickness.label: BorderThickness
SnipWindow.BorderThickness.help:
Border thickness in pixels, applied as a Gui margin on each side.

Also sets the floor for EdgeGrabZone: the grabbable band is automatically widened to at least the border thickness so a thick border stays fully grabbable for Alt-drag resizing.

SnipWindow.Bevel3D.label: Bevel3D
SnipWindow.Bevel3D.help:
Give the snip border a 3D 'floating' bevel: top and left edges lighter, bottom and right edges darker, both derived from BorderColor.

Looks best with thin borders of 1 to 2 px. Automatically disabled above Bevel3DMaxThickness, since thick beveled frames tend to look chunky.

SnipWindow.Bevel3DMaxThickness.label: Bevel3DMaxThickness
SnipWindow.Bevel3DMaxThickness.help:
Border thickness above which the 3D bevel is switched off automatically.

A bevel reads as a bevel only while the frame is thin; past this width it just looks like a chunky coloured slab, so the effect is dropped rather than drawn badly.

SnipWindow.Bevel3DStrength.label: Bevel3DStrength
SnipWindow.Bevel3DStrength.help:
How much lighter or darker the bevel edges are on the ACTIVE (focused) snip. A decimal from 0.0 to 1.0 - the fraction blended toward white for the light edges and toward black for the dark edges.

Active and inactive snips use the same bevel strength and contrast. The visual difference between them comes from Bevel3DInactiveDarknessFactor instead.

SnipWindow.Bevel3DInactiveStrength.label: Bevel3DInactiveStrength
SnipWindow.Bevel3DInactiveStrength.help:
The same bevel blend fraction as Bevel3DStrength, but for the INACTIVE (unfocused) snip. A decimal from 0.0 to 1.0.

Shipped equal to Bevel3DStrength on purpose: the active and inactive snips keep identical bevel contrast and shape, and the focus cue comes entirely from Bevel3DInactiveDarknessFactor dimming both edges together.

SnipWindow.Bevel3DInactiveDarknessFactor.label: Bevel3DInactiveDarknessFactor
SnipWindow.Bevel3DInactiveDarknessFactor.help:
How much darker BOTH bevel edges - light and dark - get on an inactive, unfocused snip. A decimal from 0.0 to 1.0.

For example 0.2 means both edges are 20 percent darker than they would be on the active snip: the same contrast and shape, just dimmed overall. That gives a focus cue without needing a second border color.

Set to 0.0 for no visual difference between focused and unfocused snips.

SnipWindow.TransColor.label: TransColor
SnipWindow.TransColor.help:
Transparent color key used to hide the corners of rotated snips. Six hex digits RRGGBB with no 0x prefix.

Magenta by default, chosen because it almost never appears naturally in screen captures - which avoids accidental see-through holes inside the image itself. Change it only if you routinely capture magenta content.

Known issue: during rotation, at angles other than 90, 180 and 270 degrees, a magenta halo of pixels can appear around the edge of the snip.

SnipShadow.ShowSnipShadow.label: ShowSnipShadow
SnipShadow.ShowSnipShadow.help:
Cast a soft translucent drop shadow to the bottom-right of each snip? This is the default for NEW snips; each snip can be toggled at runtime from its right-click Shadow menu item.

The shadow is a separate click-through window sitting just behind the snip, kept glued to it via WM_WINDOWPOSCHANGED - the snip window itself is never touched. It is painted per-pixel with UpdateLayeredWindow for real feathered alpha.

It is suppressed automatically at skewed or non-cardinal angles, where a rectangle would not match a tilted snip, and whenever the snip is not fully opaque, since a shadow behind a see-through snip looks wrong.

SnipShadow.ShadowColor.label: ShadowColor
SnipShadow.ShadowColor.help:
Shadow color, six hex digits RRGGBB with no 0x prefix. For example 000000 for black or 203040 for slate.

The GDI+ fill needs a numeric RGB value, so an AHK color name will not work here - hex only.

SnipShadow.ShadowOffset.label: ShadowOffset
SnipShadow.ShadowOffset.help:
How far in logical pixels the shadow is offset down and to the right. DPI-scaled like the rest of the snip geometry.

Keep this at or above ShadowBlur for a clean bottom-right drop. If the blur exceeds the offset you get a soft all-around halo or glow instead of a directional shadow.

SnipShadow.ShadowOffsetInactive.label: ShadowOffsetInactive
SnipShadow.ShadowOffsetInactive.help:
Shadow offset used when the snip is NOT the focused window.

Making it smaller than ShadowOffset lets an inactive snip cast a shorter shadow, which reads as sitting closer to the desktop - so the focused snip visually lifts forward. Same trick the Bevel3D active and inactive strengths use.

Set equal to ShadowOffset for no active/inactive difference.

SnipShadow.ShadowBlur.label: ShadowBlur
SnipShadow.ShadowBlur.help:
Edge softness in logical pixels. 0 gives a crisp rectangle, 5 to 8 gives a gentle feathered drop shadow, larger is softer and wider.

Softening is done with plain GDI+ bilinear scaling - a downscale and upscale pass, no effects API and no machine code - so it works everywhere.

SnipShadow.ShadowAlpha.label: ShadowAlpha
SnipShadow.ShadowAlpha.help:
Peak shadow opacity at the core: 0 is invisible, 255 is solid. The feather fades below this.

Roughly 90 to 120 works out to 35 to 47 percent, which reads as a shadow over most backdrops without turning into a black smudge.

Gestures.PanDragDivisor.label: PanDragDivisor
Gestures.PanDragDivisor.help:
Right-drag pan sensitivity: how many pixels of right-mouse drag map to ONE pixel of region pan. Hand-tool style, so the image follows the cursor.

Higher is finer and slower, which suits nudging an edge into place. 1 gives 1:1 tracking.

The fractional remainder is carried between frames, so even a slow drag moves smoothly instead of stair-stepping.

Gestures.PanClickSlop.label: PanClickSlop
Gestures.PanClickSlop.help:
Total right-drag travel in screen pixels below which the gesture is treated as a right-CLICK and opens the context menu instead of panning.

This is the dead zone at the start of any right-drag that distinguishes a deliberate pan from a plain right-click. Raise it if the menu opens when you meant to pan; lower it if you have to travel too far before panning starts.

Gestures.EdgeGrabZone.label: EdgeGrabZone
Gestures.EdgeGrabZone.help:
How far inward in pixels the grabbable band reaches from each edge of a snip, for Alt+drag edge resizing (grow or shrink the capture region, with the opposite edge staying put).

Automatically widened to at least BorderThickness so a thick border is still fully grabbable.

Only active on upright snips at 0 degrees. A rotated snip's edges do not map cleanly onto the capture rectangle, so edge resizing is suppressed there - the same rule the border follows.

Gestures.ResizeDragDivisor.label: ResizeDragDivisor
Gestures.ResizeDragDivisor.help:
Alt+Right-drag resize sensitivity: how many pixels of resize map to ONE pixel of region drag.

Higher is finer and slower, which suits nudging an edge into place. 1 gives 1:1 tracking.

The fractional remainder is carried between frames, so even a slow drag resizes smoothly instead of stair-stepping.

Straighten.StraightenStep.label: StraightenStep
Straighten.StraightenStep.help:
Degrees of deskew per Alt+comma / Alt+period.

Straighten rotates the IMAGE inside a fixed rectangular frame - for example to square up a skewed table before OCR. Unlike Rotate, which turns the whole snip frame and all, Straighten leaves the frame axis-aligned and only tilts the content within it. You then trim the exposed corners with an Alt+drag resize.

The content pivots about the centre of the crop AS IT WAS when you began straightening, and that pivot is held fixed until you return to level. So panning slides the frame over one stable rotated image with no swirl, while the tilt still turns about what you are actually looking at.

Straighten.StraightenFineStep.label: StraightenFineStep
Straighten.StraightenFineStep.help: Degrees of deskew per Shift+Alt+comma / Shift+Alt+period - the fine, sub-degree step for the last bit of squaring up.

Straighten.StraightenMaxAngle.label: StraightenMaxAngle
Straighten.StraightenMaxAngle.help:
Hard clamp on total deskew, in degrees either side of level.

The practical limit is usually CaptureAdjustMargin rather than this number: the tilt pulls surrounding pixels in from the frozen master snapshot, so a larger margin allows a larger clean straighten before the corners run past the snapshot edge.

Saving.SaveDefaultFolder.label: SaveDefaultFolder
Saving.SaveDefaultFolder.help:
Folder the Save Image As dialog opens in the first time you use it in a session. After that, the last folder you actually saved to is remembered for the rest of the session.

%USERPROFILE% is expanded. If the folder does not exist, ScreenSnip falls back to My Documents.

Saving.SaveDefaultExt.label: SaveDefaultExt
Saving.SaveDefaultExt.help:
Image format offered by default in the Save Image As dialog, and used when you type a filename with no extension.

PNG gets clean transparent corners on tilted snips. JPG and BMP have no alpha channel, so they save exactly as displayed - including the magenta corner fill on a rotated snip.

Tooltips.EnhanceToolTips.label: EnhanceToolTips
Tooltips.EnhanceToolTips.help:
Master switch for the enhanced tooltip styling provided by Resources\ToolTipOptions.ahk (by AHK forum member 'just me').

Several add-ons report status with a plain ToolTip: the OCR 'Reading...' and result messages, the AI module's progress, the Imgur toast, and the window info that follows the cursor during a Freeze Capture. Windows' default tooltip is a small pale-yellow box in an 8pt system font - easy to miss on a busy screen and hard to read at a glance.

ToolTipOptions subclasses the tooltip window CLASS, so every setting in this section applies to every ToolTip the script raises, from any module, with no change to a single ToolTip call anywhere.

Switch this off to keep plain system tooltips without deleting the file - handy for an A/B look, or if a theming tool already styles tooltips. Deleting Resources\ToolTipOptions.ahk has the same effect, since it is included with the *i flag.

Tooltips.TipFontName.label: TipFontName
Tooltips.TipFontName.help:
Font family for tooltips. Any installed font name, or blank for the system default face.

A monospaced face such as Consolas or Cascadia Mono is worth considering: the OCR modules dump captured TEXT into these tooltips, and columns from a table grab line up far better in a fixed-pitch font.

Tooltips.TipFontSize.label: TipFontSize
Tooltips.TipFontSize.help:
Tooltip point size. 11 to 13 is a comfortable step up from the roughly 8pt Windows default; the module accepts anything from 1 to 255, so go large if you want it unmissable.

The styling is applied AFTER ScreenSnip's DPI-awareness call, because point size is converted to pixels through GetDeviceCaps and that reading depends on the thread's DPI awareness. Set the font first and a 12pt tooltip comes out noticeably small on a scaled display.

Tooltips.TipFontStyle.label: TipFontStyle
Tooltips.TipFontStyle.help:
Extra font styles, space separated, from: bold, italic, underline, strike, norm. Also accepts wNNN for weight (1 to 1000) and qN for quality (0 to 5). Leave blank for none.

Colour options such as cRED are ignored here - use TipTextColor instead.

A bad style word or an out-of-range size makes SetFont throw. ScreenSnip catches that, resets tooltips to the plain Windows style for the session, and tells you once rather than taking the script down.

Tooltips.TipBackColor.label: TipBackColor
Tooltips.TipBackColor.help:
Tooltip background color: an AHK color name such as Yellow, or six hex digits RRGGBB with no 0x prefix.

Set BOTH this and TipTextColor to blank to keep Windows' own tooltip colours while still changing the font and margins.

Shipped tracking FreezeHintBackColor so the freeze hint and the status tooltips read as one UI - the same reason BorderColor tracks SelectionColor.

Tooltips.TipTextColor.label: TipTextColor
Tooltips.TipTextColor.help:
Tooltip text color: an AHK color name such as Black, or six hex digits RRGGBB with no 0x prefix.

Set BOTH this and TipBackColor to blank to keep Windows' own tooltip colours while still changing the font and margins.

Shipped tracking FreezeHintTextColor so the freeze hint and the status tooltips read as one UI.

Tooltips.TipMarginL.label: TipMarginL
Tooltips.TipMarginL.help:
Tooltip interior padding on the LEFT, in pixels.

The default Windows tooltip is cramped; a few pixels of breathing room helps legibility about as much as the bigger font does.

Set all four margins to 0 to use Windows' own spacing.

Tooltips.TipMarginT.label: TipMarginT
Tooltips.TipMarginT.help:
Tooltip interior padding on the TOP, in pixels.

Set all four margins to 0 to use Windows' own spacing.

Tooltips.TipMarginR.label: TipMarginR
Tooltips.TipMarginR.help:
Tooltip interior padding on the RIGHT, in pixels.

Set all four margins to 0 to use Windows' own spacing.

Tooltips.TipMarginB.label: TipMarginB
Tooltips.TipMarginB.help:
Tooltip interior padding on the BOTTOM, in pixels.

Set all four margins to 0 to use Windows' own spacing.

Tooltips.TipTitle.label: TipTitle
Tooltips.TipTitle.help:
Optional bold title line shown above the tooltip text. Blank means no title bar at all.

Blank is the default deliberately: a title is a lot of chrome for a two-word status message, and it would also appear on the cursor-following window info during a Freeze Capture, where it would just be in the way.

Tooltips.TipTitleIcon.label: TipTitleIcon
Tooltips.TipTitleIcon.help:
Icon shown beside the tooltip title. Ignored entirely when TipTitle is blank.

0 = none, 1 = info, 2 = warning, 3 = error. Add 3 for the large versions: 4 = large info, 5 = large warning, 6 = large error.

SnipOCR.OcrPaddleExe.label: OcrPaddleExe
SnipOCR.OcrPaddleExe.help:
Full path to PaddleOCR-json.exe. The 'models' folder MUST be its sibling - the engine is launched with that folder as its working directory, which is how OcrLangConfig resolves.

A relative path is resolved against the ScreenSnip.ahk folder, so the shipped default points into Resources\.

Setup: download PaddleOCR-json (Windows x64) from https://github.com/hiroi-sora/PaddleOCR-json/releases/latest and unzip it into Resources\. You want the folder containing PaddleOCR-json.exe AND the models subfolder; they must stay together.

Requires a CPU with AVX (any modern Core or Ryzen). If yours lacks it, use RapidOCR-json instead - same JSON output, same code works.

Only the PaddleOCR menu items need this. Copy Text (Windows) uses Descolada's OCR.ahk and needs no engine install.

SnipOCR.OcrLangConfig.label: OcrLangConfig
SnipOCR.OcrLangConfig.help:
Language config file, RELATIVE to the PaddleOCR engine folder - not to ScreenSnip.

The engine defaults to Simplified Chinese if this is blank, so leave it set for English.

Others shipped in the release: models\config_chinese_cht.txt, models\config_japan.txt, models\config_korean.txt.

SnipOCR.OcrUpscale.label: OcrUpscale
SnipOCR.OcrUpscale.help:
Bicubic upscale factor applied before OCR. 1 disables it.

Screen text is typically 10 to 14 pixels tall, right at the edge of what OCR engines handle well. Upscaling to 2x or 3x makes a large accuracy difference and costs almost nothing.

If a large snip at 3x is getting slow, lower this rather than capping OcrMaxSideLen.

SnipOCR.OcrLimitSideLen.label: OcrLimitSideLen
SnipOCR.OcrLimitSideLen.help:
Paddle DOWNSIZES any image whose long edge exceeds this - which silently undoes the upscaling above and is a very easy way to sabotage yourself. A 3x upscale of a modest snip lands around 5000px, so a fixed 2880 here would shrink it straight back to an effective 1.7x.

0 = AUTO: size the limit to the image so no downscaling ever happens. This is what you want.

Set a fixed number only to deliberately cap it.

SnipOCR.OcrMaxSideLen.label: OcrMaxSideLen
SnipOCR.OcrMaxSideLen.help:
Safety ceiling for AUTO mode (OcrLimitSideLen = 0).

Detection cost scales with area, so a huge snip at 3x could get slow. If the image exceeds this, Paddle will shrink it - and the right response is usually to lower OcrUpscale instead of raising this.

SnipOCR.OcrRotateFill.label: OcrRotateFill
SnipOCR.OcrRotateFill.help:
Fill color for the triangular corners exposed when a fine-rotated snip is sent to OCR. Six hex digits RRGGBB with no 0x prefix.

On screen those corners use the magenta color key, but for OCR we use white so they read as blank page rather than as content.

Set to 000000 if you routinely OCR light-on-dark text.

SnipOCR.OcrMinScore.label: OcrMinScore
SnipOCR.OcrMinScore.help:
Discard text blocks whose confidence is below this, from 0.0 to 1.0.

The default of 0 - keep everything - is deliberate. A confidence filter would earn its keep if a junk block could SHIFT your data, but it cannot: every block is snapped to a column anchor, so dropping one leaves a hole and moves nothing. Filtering therefore buys no safety and costs real cells.

And a hole is worse than a typo. A misread value is visible and fixable; a dropped one just looks like a legitimately empty cell. On a real 21x20 table, a MinScore of 0.5 silently discarded 41 percent of it.

Only raise this if you are OCRing prose and want to suppress noise.

SnipOCR.OcrMarkBelow.label: OcrMarkBelow
SnipOCR.OcrMarkBelow.help:
If above 0, append a question mark to any cell whose confidence is below this value (0.0 to 1.0), so you can find the shaky ones in Excel with Ctrl+F.

Note this makes those cells TEXT rather than numbers, so leave it at 0 for tables you will compute on.

SnipOCR.OcrRowTol.label: OcrRowTol
SnipOCR.OcrRowTol.help:
Row clustering tolerance. Two text blocks land in the same ROW if their vertical centres are within (OcrRowTol x median block height) of each other.

PaddleOCR returns loose text blocks with bounding boxes, NOT a table - the grid is rebuilt by clustering those boxes. This tolerance is expressed as a fraction of the median text-block HEIGHT so it scales automatically with font size and with OcrUpscale.

Raise it if a single visual row is being split in two; lower it if two rows are merging.

SnipOCR.OcrColTol.label: OcrColTol
SnipOCR.OcrColTol.help:
Column clustering tolerance. Two text blocks land in the same COLUMN if their left edges are within (OcrColTol x median block height) of each other.

Like OcrRowTol, expressed as a fraction of median text-block height so it scales with font size and OcrUpscale.

Raise it if one column is being split in two; lower it if two columns are merging.

SnipOCR.OcrReflow.label: OcrReflow
SnipOCR.OcrReflow.help:
Stitch wrapped cells back together?

A cell whose text wraps onto several lines arrives as several separate blocks, so a 5-row table can come out as 31 rows. Reflow puts them back.

How it decides: it measures the WHITESPACE between consecutive rows, not centre-to-centre pitch, which is contaminated by text height. In a table with wrapped cells those gaps are strongly bimodal - small ones are line spacing inside a cell, large ones are actual row borders. In a table with no wrapping they are all the same size. So the gaps are split into two groups and reflow only happens if the large group is clearly larger than the small one; otherwise every row is left alone.

On real tables the separation is obvious: ratio 2.3 for a wrapped rubric, 1.6 for an unwrapped number grid.

SnipOCR.OcrReflowRatio.label: OcrReflowRatio
SnipOCR.OcrReflowRatio.help:
How much bigger the 'row border' gaps must be than the 'line spacing' gaps before we believe the table has wrapped cells at all.

Lower is more eager to reflow. Below about 1.6 you risk merging genuinely separate rows.

SnipOCR.OcrReflowAnchorCol.label: OcrReflowAnchorCol
SnipOCR.OcrReflowAnchorCol.help:
The anchor (key) column - the one holding a label on every logical row and blank on wrapped continuation lines. Column 1 in almost every table.

This exists because GAPS ALONE ARE NOT ENOUGH, and a real document proved it. On a scanned IEP service grid an 85px gap sat INSIDE a cell - a faint dash the engine never detected left a hole - while a genuine row border was only 39px. The geometry lied. But column 1, reading '1,2 / 2 / ALL / 3 / 4', did not. So a new logical row must satisfy BOTH tests: a big gap above it AND content in the anchor column.

Set to 0 to use gaps alone. Falls back to gaps automatically if the anchor column turns out to be too sparse to group by.

SnipOCR.OcrReflowGapFactor.label: OcrReflowGapFactor
SnipOCR.OcrReflowGapFactor.help: A gap counts as 'big' - that is, a candidate row border rather than in-cell line spacing - if it exceeds this multiple of the median row gap.

SnipOCR.OcrNotATableWarn.label: OcrNotATableWarn
SnipOCR.OcrNotATableWarn.help:
The 'this is not a table' guard. If more than this fraction of the text sits in one column, the snip is almost certainly prose or a form rather than a grid - and Copy Text will do a far better job than Copy Table, so you get a prompt.

Measured on real documents: a numeric grid ran 7 percent, a rubric 27 percent, a scanned service matrix 40 percent, but a one-column form with bullets hit 77 percent.

Set to 0 to disable the prompt.

SnipOCR.OcrDebug.label: OcrDebug
SnipOCR.OcrDebug.help:
Write three diagnostic files into the Data folder on every PaddleOCR run, stamped with the run time:

SnipOCR_<stamp>_image.png - what the engine was actually fed
SnipOCR_<stamp>_raw.json - what the engine returned
SnipOCR_<stamp>_blocks.txt - how the blocks were clustered

The blocks dump is the useful one: it tells you whether a wrong table is the ENGINE misreading the text or the CLUSTERING misplacing it, which you cannot tell from the TSV alone.

Leave off for normal use - these files accumulate.

SnipAI.AiModel.label: AiModel
SnipAI.AiModel.help:
Any vision-capable OpenAI chat model. If the one you name is not enabled on your account you get a clear 'model not found' back from the API - the error body is shown verbatim, so it is a one-line fix.

This is the DEFAULT. A Model= line under [OpenAI] in Data\ApiKeys.ini overrides it, so a model can be swapped without touching this file - handy for A/B testing quality against cost.

Do NOT reflexively drop to a 'mini' tier model the way you might for a text-only task. Table extraction from a scan is dense small digits and fine ruling lines, which is exactly where the cheap tiers degrade - and they degrade into plausible-looking WRONG NUMBERS, not obvious errors. Measure first: switch on AiShowTokenUsage and see where the money actually goes before trading accuracy for it.

Note that this module sends the image OFF YOUR MACHINE and costs money - fractions of a cent per snip. OpenAI prepaid credits expire after one year.

SnipAI.AiDetail.label: AiDetail
SnipAI.AiDetail.help:
Image detail level sent to the vision model.

high - tiles the image and reads fine print. This is what you want for OCR.
low - sends a single coarse thumbnail for about a tenth the cost.

SnipAI.AiMaxSide.label: AiMaxSide
SnipAI.AiMaxSide.help:
Longest edge in pixels the snip is scaled down to before upload.

The API scales anything larger down before tiling, so sending a bigger image than this is pure upload time with no accuracy gain.

Unlike the local OCR path there is no reason to UPSCALE for the AI - the model is not helped by it.

SnipAI.AiResolveTimeout.label: AiResolveTimeout
SnipAI.AiResolveTimeout.help:
WinHttp DNS name-resolution timeout in milliseconds.

One of four timeouts - resolve, connect, send, receive - that were a single Timeouts array in SnipAI.ahk and are split out here so each can be edited on its own.

SnipAI.AiConnectTimeout.label: AiConnectTimeout
SnipAI.AiConnectTimeout.help: WinHttp connection timeout in milliseconds - how long to wait to establish the connection to the API.

SnipAI.AiSendTimeout.label: AiSendTimeout
SnipAI.AiSendTimeout.help:
WinHttp send timeout in milliseconds - how long the request upload may take.

The payload is a base64-encoded PNG, so this scales with AiMaxSide. Raise it if you work on a slow uplink with large snips.

SnipAI.AiReceiveTimeout.label: AiReceiveTimeout
SnipAI.AiReceiveTimeout.help:
WinHttp receive timeout in milliseconds.

This one in particular must be generous: vision calls are slow, and a dense table can take a while to come back. This is the real ceiling on how long a wedged request can hang.

SnipAI.AiWaitSecs.label: AiWaitSecs
SnipAI.AiWaitSecs.help:
Seconds to wait for the complete response, passed to WaitForResponse.

Keep this roughly in step with AiReceiveTimeout - expressed in seconds rather than milliseconds - so the two do not fight each other.

SnipAI.AiGroundWithOcr.label: AiGroundWithOcr
SnipAI.AiGroundWithOcr.help:
Run PaddleOCR first and pass its text to the model as a spelling reference?

Costs one extra engine run - a second or two, offline. Silently skipped if SnipOCR.ahk is absent or the engine is not installed.

What gets sent is Paddle's reading-order LINES, not its reconstructed grid. That is deliberate: sending the grid would hand the model the very column mistake this feature exists to correct. The accompanying preamble grants the OCR authority over CHARACTERS and explicitly strips it of any authority over LAYOUT.

The reason Copy Table (AI) beats Copy Table (Paddle) at all is that a vision model can see the table's RULING LINES, which no box-based OCR engine can.

SnipAI.AiNormalizeTablePunct.label: AiNormalizeTablePunct
SnipAI.AiNormalizeTablePunct.help:
Fold en dashes, em dashes, curly quotes and non-breaking spaces down to plain ASCII in table cells, so what lands on the clipboard pastes cleanly into a spreadsheet.

Table cells ONLY. Copy Text (AI) always stays verbatim.

SnipAI.AiDashCellToEmpty.label: AiDashCellToEmpty
SnipAI.AiDashCellToEmpty.help:
Blank out any cell whose entire content is a dash.

In most printed tables a lone dash is a 'no data' marker rather than a value, and blanking it keeps a numeric column numeric in Excel.

Off by default because it IS a content change, and in some tables a dash means something specific.

SnipAI.AiShowTokenUsage.label: AiShowTokenUsage
SnipAI.AiShowTokenUsage.help:
Append the token counts from the last call to the result tooltip.

Costs nothing, and turns 'roughly two cents a table' into a number you can act on. In particular it separates image tokens from output tokens from reasoning tokens - the last of which are billed but otherwise invisible.

Worth switching on before you decide whether a cheaper model is worth the accuracy loss.

SnipAI.AiDebug.label: AiDebug
SnipAI.AiDebug.help:
Keep the temporary PNG and write the raw request and response into the Data folder, so a failed call can be inspected.

The request dump does NOT contain your API key - that rides in a header, not the body - but it DOES contain the base64 image, so the file will be large.

Leave off for normal use.

SnipImgur.ImgurConfirmBeforeUpload.label: ImgurConfirmBeforeUpload
SnipImgur.ImgurConfirmBeforeUpload.help:
Ask 'are you sure?' before the one-click Imgur > Upload menu item?

An upload is PUBLIC to anyone with the link, and an anonymous upload can only be deleted during the session that made it - once ScreenSnip exits it is effectively permanent. That is a lot of consequence for one menu click on a snip that might be showing an e-mail or a password field, so this defaults to on.

Switch it off once the flow feels familiar.

SnipImgur.ImgurDefaultFormat.label: ImgurDefaultFormat
SnipImgur.ImgurDefaultFormat.help:
Link format placed on the clipboard by the one-click upload, and pre-selected in the Uploader's 'Copy as' dropdown.

Imgur's API returns a link to the image's PAGE, which carries a nav bar. Forum [img] tags and HTML img tags need the DIRECT file, which is derived from the response's id and type fields.

'BBCode thumbnail linked' uses Imgur's 640x640 thumbnail so a big screenshot does not blow out a forum thread's layout. Note that Imgur's thumbnails of an animated image are STILL frames, so you get a motionless preview linking through to the moving version.

The last two options only mean anything for an animated upload. On a still image they quietly fall back to the direct link rather than handing back a URL to a video that does not exist.
SnipImgur.ImgurDefaultFormat.validation: Direct link|BBCode [img]|BBCode thumbnail linked|Markdown|HTML img tag|Page link|Direct MP4  (animated only)|HTML5 video tag  (animated only)

SnipImgur.ImgurProgressDelayMs.label: ImgurProgressDelayMs
SnipImgur.ImgurProgressDelayMs.help:
Milliseconds an upload must run before the small progress and Cancel window appears.

Small uploads finish faster than this and never flash a dialog at you.

SnipImgur.ImgurResolveTimeout.label: ImgurResolveTimeout
SnipImgur.ImgurResolveTimeout.help:
WinHttp DNS name-resolution timeout in milliseconds.

The Imgur timeouts are deliberately much tighter than the AI ones: a stalled upload is more annoying than a slow vision call, and there is a Cancel button behind it.

SnipImgur.ImgurConnectTimeout.label: ImgurConnectTimeout
SnipImgur.ImgurConnectTimeout.help: WinHttp connection timeout in milliseconds - how long to wait to establish the connection to Imgur.

SnipImgur.ImgurSendTimeout.label: ImgurSendTimeout
SnipImgur.ImgurSendTimeout.help:
WinHttp send timeout in milliseconds - how long the upload itself may take.

The image is posted as a base64 form field, which inflates the payload by roughly a third. Raise this if you upload large animated GIFs over a slow uplink.

The API caps out around 10 MB on disc regardless - that is the JSON API's limit, not the website's 20 MB.

SnipImgur.ImgurReceiveTimeout.label: ImgurReceiveTimeout
SnipImgur.ImgurReceiveTimeout.help:
WinHttp receive timeout in milliseconds.

This is the real ceiling on how long a wedged upload can last if you do not hit Cancel.

SnipWinDetect.WinDetectEnabled.label: WinDetectEnabled
SnipWinDetect.WinDetectEnabled.help:
Master switch for hover-to-highlight window detection during Freeze Capture, SnagIt style: move the mouse over the frozen screen and the window beneath the cursor is outlined; left-click captures it whole. Right-drag still does the normal freehand region selection, unchanged.

Off means the module stays loaded but never highlights anything, and Freeze Capture behaves exactly as it did before.

How it works, and why it is not image analysis: the frozen backdrop is only a PICTURE laid over the desktop. The real windows are still sitting underneath at the same coordinates, so the window tree is simply queried - no edge detection on the bitmap required. Because the screen is frozen nothing can move, so the whole top-level window list is snapshotted ONCE when the freeze begins and every mouse-move is then just an in-memory rectangle test.

Scope is TOP-LEVEL WINDOWS only, plus each monitor. Child controls are not detected: modern apps such as Chrome, Electron, UWP and WPF draw everything inside a single HWND and would need UI Automation on top of per-control enumeration.

SnipWinDetect.WinDetectColor.label: WinDetectColor
SnipWinDetect.WinDetectColor.help:
color of the highlight outline drawn around the detected window. Six hex digits RRGGBB with no 0x prefix.

This needs to read clearly against an arbitrary screenshot. A saturated blue does that better than red or green, both of which disappear into common window chrome.

SnipWinDetect.WinDetectThickness.label: WinDetectThickness
SnipWinDetect.WinDetectThickness.help:
Outline thickness in pixels.

Automatically thinned for windows too small to fit it, so a tiny tooltip still shows an outline rather than a solid block of color.

SnipWinDetect.WinDetectPollMs.label: WinDetectPollMs
SnipWinDetect.WinDetectPollMs.help:
Cursor poll interval in milliseconds.

The hit test itself is a memory scan against the snapshot taken when the freeze began, so this is cheap. 40 ms is about 25 fps and feels immediate. Values below 10 are clamped.

SnipWinDetect.WinDetectMinSize.label: WinDetectMinSize
SnipWinDetect.WinDetectMinSize.help:
Ignore windows smaller than this in either dimension, in pixels.

Filters out the 1x1 and 0x0 message-only oddities that a lot of apps leave lying around, which would otherwise be highlightable targets.

SnipWinDetect.WinDetectShowInfo.label: WinDetectShowInfo
SnipWinDetect.WinDetectShowInfo.help:
Show the floating title, class and size readout beside the cursor while hovering during a Freeze Capture?

Useful for confirming you are about to grab the window you think you are, particularly when several are stacked.

SnipWinDetect.WinDetectTipIndex.label: WinDetectTipIndex
SnipWinDetect.WinDetectTipIndex.help:
ToolTip slot number used for the cursor-following window readout.

AHK supports 20 independent tooltip slots. ScreenSnip itself raises no ToolTips of its own, so this only matters if another add-on starts using the same slot and the two overwrite each other.

SnipWinDetect.WinDetectIncludeDesktop.label: WinDetectIncludeDesktop
SnipWinDetect.WinDetectIncludeDesktop.help:
Treat the desktop itself (the Progman and WorkerW windows) as a capture target?

Off by default: the desktop is screen-sized and sits under everything, so including it means the highlight never goes away over empty desktop and Progman swallows hit tests that should have missed.

If you want a whole-screen target, use WinDetectIncludeMonitors instead - it gets you the same thing without the side effects.

SnipWinDetect.WinDetectIncludeMonitors.label: WinDetectIncludeMonitors
SnipWinDetect.WinDetectIncludeMonitors.help:
Offer each MONITOR as a capture target as well as the windows?

Monitors are appended AFTER the windows, so they sit at the bottom of the Z-ordered candidate list. That gives you three good properties at once: a real window under the cursor always wins, a whole screen is always one wheel-step past the last window, and empty desktop still has something to highlight - all without switching WinDetectIncludeDesktop on.

Captures full monitor bounds, taskbar included.

Puzzle.GridCols.label: GridCols
Puzzle.GridCols.help:
Columns the snip is cut into when a puzzle is started from the Play item at the top of the Slide Puzzle or Swap Puzzle submenu.

The explicit sizes on that submenu (3 x 3 through 6 x 6) ignore this, as does Custom Size. This is only the default the Play item uses, and the size a puzzle returns to if you have not chosen otherwise.

Clamped to 2 through 12 in code, whatever is typed here.

Puzzle.GridRows.label: GridRows
Puzzle.GridRows.help:
Rows the snip is cut into. See GridCols - the two are read together and the same notes apply.

Rows and columns are independent, so a wide snip can be cut 6 x 3 if that suits it better than a square grid. Clamped to 2 through 12.

Puzzle.MaxBoardSize.label: MaxBoardSize
Puzzle.MaxBoardSize.help:
Largest the board is allowed to be, measured on its longest side in pixels.

0 means NO CAP, which is the default and almost certainly what you want: a tile puzzle is nothing but the picture, so shrinking it throws away the detail you are matching on. Unlike the jigsaw there is no scatter area to find room for, just a few pixels of window frame.

The screen is the real limit either way. The board is always fitted to the monitor work area, because an oversized puzzle window cannot be resized once it is open. Set a pixel value here only if you want puzzles smaller than your screen would allow.

Puzzle.MinBoardSize.label: MinBoardSize
Puzzle.MinBoardSize.help:
Smallest the board may be, on its longest side in pixels. A snip smaller than this is scaled UP to reach it.

This exists so that a tiny snip - a toolbar button, a few words of text - still produces tiles big enough to click. It costs sharpness, since the picture is being enlarged past its native size, but an unclickable puzzle is worse.

Only ever enlarges. Snips already larger than this are untouched.

Puzzle.TileGap.label: TileGap
Puzzle.TileGap.help:
Pixels of board color showing between tiles, giving the grid its cut-apart look.

The gap is taken out of the tile image itself, like the kerf of a saw, so those pixels are not shown anywhere while the puzzle is unsolved. They reappear the moment it is solved, which is why the seams visibly heal at the end.

0 puts the tiles flush together. On a very fine grid over a small snip the gap self-limits to 0 rather than eating the tile.

Puzzle.ShowNumbers.label: ShowNumbers
Puzzle.ShowNumbers.help:
Number each tile in its top-left corner, showing where it belongs.

Makes both puzzles markedly easier, and turns a picture puzzle into a logic one. Useful on a snip that is mostly flat color and hard to solve by image alone.

Numbers are baked into the tile images rather than drawn each frame, so toggling this in game (the N key, or the right-click menu) rebuilds the tile set. That takes a few milliseconds and is not noticeable.

Puzzle.SlideAnimMs.label: SlideAnimMs
Puzzle.SlideAnimMs.help:
How long a tile takes to travel one cell, in milliseconds. Applies to both puzzles despite the name - it is also the duration of a swap crossover.

Anything below 10 turns the animation off and moves become instant. Worth trying if a very large board feels sluggish: every animation frame rebuilds a bitmap the size of the whole board, so the cost grows with the picture.

Around 90 reads as responsive. Above roughly 200 it starts to feel like the board is waiting for you.

Puzzle.ShuffleMoves.label: ShuffleMoves
Puzzle.ShuffleMoves.help:
How many slides to make when shuffling a SLIDE puzzle. 0 means auto, which is 25 times the tile count - 400 slides for a 4 x 4.

The shuffle is made of real, legal slides rather than a random rearrangement, and that is what guarantees the board can be solved. A randomly permuted sliding puzzle is solvable only half the time, because half of all arrangements are unreachable; walking the gap around at random can only ever reach positions it can walk back from.

Setting this low (say 20) gives a nearly-solved board, which is the quickest way to test that the win detection and the fanfare still work.

Has NO effect on the swap puzzle. Adjacent swaps can reach every arrangement, so that one is shuffled by a straight random deal with nothing to tune.

Puzzle.BoardColor.label: BoardColor
Puzzle.BoardColor.help:
color behind the tiles, seen through the gaps between them and in the empty cell of a slide puzzle.

Six hex digits, RRGGBB, with no 0x or # prefix.

A dark neutral works best. The tiles carry a screenshot, so a strong color here competes with the picture rather than framing it. Only visible at all if TileGap is above 0.

Puzzle.TileOutline.label: TileOutline
Puzzle.TileOutline.help:
Draw a hairline edge around each tile - a touch of dark on the outside and a touch of light just inside it, a cheap bevel.

Worth keeping on. Without it, adjacent tiles showing similar parts of the picture merge into one another and the grid becomes hard to read, especially with TileGap at 0 or 1.

Baked into the tile images, so this is read when the tiles are built.

Puzzle.SelectColor.label: SelectColor
Puzzle.SelectColor.help:
color of the ring around the picked-up tile in the SWAP puzzle. Unused by the slide puzzle, which has no selection.

Six hex digits, RRGGBB, with no 0x or # prefix.

The ring is drawn as four nested rectangles - a bright core with darker lines outside and inside it - so it stays visible over both pale and dark tiles. Keep whatever you choose saturated: a mid grey would vanish against half the snips you might play.

Puzzle.CloseSnipOnStart.label: CloseSnipOnStart
Puzzle.CloseSnipOnStart.help:
Close the snip when a puzzle is made from it, so the snip appears to turn into the puzzle.

Off by default, and off is the kinder setting: the snip stays open beside the board as your reference picture. The puzzle window deliberately opens offset down and right so it does not cover it.

Turning this on is not punishing - hold Space or use the Peek button to see the finished picture at any time - but the snip itself is gone for good.

Puzzle.SoundOnSolve.label: SoundOnSolve
Puzzle.SoundOnSolve.help:
Play a three-note fanfare when the puzzle is solved.

Uses SoundBeep, so it comes from the motherboard speaker path rather than the sound card and ignores your volume mixer. It fires on its own thread so the board is already repainted when it plays.

Puzzle.AlwaysOnTop.label: AlwaysOnTop
Puzzle.AlwaysOnTop.help:
Keep the puzzle window above other windows.

On by default, on the reasoning that a puzzle is something you dip into between other work and losing it behind a browser is annoying. Turn it off if you would rather it behaved like an ordinary window.

Jigsaw.PieceCount.label: PieceCount
Jigsaw.PieceCount.help:
Default number of pieces, used by the Play item at the top of the Jigsaw submenu. The explicit counts on that submenu ignore this.

The number is a target, not a promise. It is turned into a grid that respects the snip's shape, so pieces come out roughly square instead of long slivers on a wide screenshot - ask for 48 on a landscape snip and you get 8 x 6, on a portrait one 6 x 8. The window title reports the count you actually got.

Clamped to 12 through 300.

Jigsaw.MaxBoardSize.label: MaxBoardSize
Jigsaw.MaxBoardSize.help:
Largest the assembled picture is allowed to be, on its longest side in pixels. This is the PICTURE, not the window - the table around it is set by CanvasScale.

0 means no cap of its own, which is the default: the picture is made as large as the screen allows once the scatter area has been accounted for. The window is always fitted to the monitor work area, since an oversized jigsaw window cannot be resized once it is open.

The picture is never scaled UP beyond its native size to fill the canvas - enlarging a screenshot just makes a blurry puzzle. MinBoardSize still rescues genuinely tiny snips.

Jigsaw.MinBoardSize.label: MinBoardSize
Jigsaw.MinBoardSize.help:
Smallest the assembled picture may be, on its longest side in pixels. A snip smaller than this is scaled up to reach it.

Same purpose as the tile puzzle's version: a tiny snip cut into 48 pieces would otherwise produce pieces too small to grab. Only ever enlarges.

Jigsaw.CanvasScale.label: CanvasScale
Jigsaw.CanvasScale.help:
Size of the table, as a percentage of the assembled picture. At 180 the gutter around the picture is 40 percent of its width on each side.

Because the window is always fitted to the screen, this is now purely a dial trading table space against picture size: a bigger gutter means a smaller picture, and a smaller gutter means the picture can be larger. On a 1080p screen a landscape snip lands near 52 percent of its original size at 180, and near 67 percent at 140.

You need less dedicated storage than a physical jigsaw, because the opening scatter spreads pieces across the whole canvas including the assembly area rather than heaping them round the edge. 140 to 150 is a good starting point if you want more picture.

Clamped to 110 through 280.

Jigsaw.SnapPixels.label: SnapPixels
Jigsaw.SnapPixels.help:
How close two pieces must be, in pixels, before they snap together. 0 means auto, which is a sixth of a piece with a floor of 10.

Snapping compares TRANSLATIONS, not absolute positions: every piece knows where it belongs in the finished picture, and two pieces are correctly placed relative to each other exactly when their offsets from home match. So the assembly can be built anywhere on the table and pieces never snap to the frame, only to each other.

Resist setting this very low. A few pixels reads as broken - you line something up by eye, let go, and nothing happens. Auto is deliberately generous enough to feel magnetic.

Jigsaw.KnobDepth.label: KnobDepth
Jigsaw.KnobDepth.help:
Height of the tab on a piece edge, as a percentage of that edge's length.

Around 22 is the classic jigsaw look. Lower gives shallow, timid tabs that are hard to read; higher gives long-necked pieces that overlap their neighbours heavily when scattered.

Every interior edge also gets random jitter on the tab's direction, position and size, which is what stops every piece looking identical. Edges are generated once per puzzle and each is shared by the two pieces that meet along it, so a tab and its socket are literally the same curve and cannot disagree.

Clamped to 8 through 40. Also sets how much bigger than its cell a piece bitmap has to be, so very large values cost memory.

Jigsaw.PieceOutline.label: PieceOutline
Jigsaw.PieceOutline.help:
Stroke a hairline outline around each piece.

Worth keeping on for a reason beyond looks: GDI+ clipping is not anti-aliased, so the cut edge of a piece comes out slightly jagged. Stroking the same path over it hides that, as well as separating pieces that overlap on the table.

Jigsaw.ShowBoardOutline.label: ShowBoardOutline
Jigsaw.ShowBoardOutline.help:
Draw a faint frame on the table showing where the finished picture will sit.

Not authentic - a real jigsaw has no such guide - but a table with no box lid and no edges is disorienting. Pieces do not snap to it and you are free to assemble anywhere; it is only a hint.

Can be toggled in game with the F key. The frame switches from a white hairline to a black one when the felt is light, so it stays visible either way.

Jigsaw.FeltColor.label: FeltColor
Jigsaw.FeltColor.help:
color of the table the pieces lie on.

Six hex digits, RRGGBB, with no 0x or # prefix.

This sets the HUE and the starting position of the Felt slider on the puzzle's toolbar. That slider walks this same color from black up to its own fully-lit version, so a dark blue-grey here gives you a range of dark blue-greys rather than a wash toward white.

The slider is session-only and does not write back here. To keep a setting you like, read the color off it and enter it here - the slider's midpoint on the default hue is around 283440.

Something dark and desaturated works best. The pieces carry a screenshot, and a strong table color fights it.

Jigsaw.SoundOnSnap.label: SoundOnSnap
Jigsaw.SoundOnSnap.help:
Play a short click when pieces join.

The main feedback that a join actually took, since a correct snap can be a small visual movement. Uses SoundBeep, so it ignores your volume mixer - turn it off if that is intrusive.

Jigsaw.SoundOnSolve.label: SoundOnSolve
Jigsaw.SoundOnSolve.help:
Play a three-note fanfare when the last pieces join.

Separate from SoundOnSnap, so you can keep the completion sound while turning off the per-join click.

Jigsaw.AlwaysOnTop.label: AlwaysOnTop
Jigsaw.AlwaysOnTop.help:
Keep the jigsaw window above other windows.

On by default. A jigsaw is a longer sitting than a tile puzzle, so this is the one most likely to be worth turning off if you want to park it behind something and come back to it.

Jigsaw.CloseSnipOnStart.label: CloseSnipOnStart
Jigsaw.CloseSnipOnStart.help:
Close the snip when a jigsaw is made from it.

Off by default so the snip stays open as your reference picture, which matters more here than in the tile puzzles - a jigsaw has no grid to reason about, only the image. Hold Space or use the Peek button to see the finished picture at any time.

Markup.Color.label: Color
Markup.Color.help:
Default STROKE color for a new markup object: the arrow, the rectangle's outline, the callout's border. Six hex digits, RRGGBB, with no 0x or # prefix.

This is only the starting value. The palette's twelve swatches change it on the fly, and with an object selected a swatch recolors THAT object (or every object in the selection) instead of the default.

Shipped as a strong red because it is the one hue almost never present in application chrome, so an annotation reads as an annotation rather than as part of the screenshot.

Markup.FillColor.label: FillColor
Markup.FillColor.help:
Default FILL color for shapes drawn with FillShapes on, and the body color of callout bubbles. Six hex digits, RRGGBB, no prefix.

Ctrl+click a palette swatch to set the fill instead of the stroke; doing so also switches the fill on.

Numbered badges ignore this and take their disc color from Color, so that recoloring a badge is one click rather than two. Text drawn on a fill (badge digits, callout text) is automatically black or white, whichever contrasts with the fill.

Markup.FillShapes.label: FillShapes
Markup.FillShapes.help:
Whether a newly drawn rectangle or ellipse starts filled with FillColor.

Off is the usual choice for annotation: an outline lets the reader see what you are pointing AT. Turn it on when you are covering something up rather than circling it, though Blur is the better tool for hiding information.

The palette's 'Fill shape' checkbox overrides this per object.

Markup.Thickness.label: Thickness
Markup.Thickness.help:
Default stroke width in image pixels for new objects: line and arrow shafts, shape outlines, callout borders.

2 to 4 suits a normal desktop screenshot. Go heavier for a scaled-down image that will be viewed small, lighter for a dense UI where a fat outline would bury the thing it is marking.

The palette's Width list changes it, and a group resize deliberately does NOT scale it - a shrunken hairline reads as a rendering fault rather than as a smaller arrow.

Markup.FontName.label: FontName
Markup.FontName.help:
Font family for text labels, numbered badges and callout text. Any installed font name.

A UI font is usually the right call, since the annotation is meant to sit on top of a screenshot without pretending to be part of it.

Markup.FontSize.label: FontSize
Markup.FontSize.help:
Default text height in IMAGE pixels, not points. A label therefore keeps its size relative to the screenshot rather than to the display, so a snip shared with someone on a different DPI looks the same to both of you.

Also drives two things that are derived from it: the diameter of a numbered badge, and the corner radius of a callout bubble.

Unlike stroke width, font size DOES scale with a multi-object group resize.

Markup.Outline.label: Outline
Markup.Outline.help:
Draw a thin contrasting halo underneath each object so it stays legible against a busy background. This is what stops a red arrow disappearing into a red-ish toolbar.

The halo is black or white, chosen from the OBJECT'S own color, not by sampling the pixels behind it - sampling is expensive and makes the halo flicker between black and white while you drag a shape across a varied screenshot.

On by default because it is doing a job, unlike the shadow, which is decoration. Per object on the palette. Highlighter strokes never get one.

Markup.OutlineWidth.label: OutlineWidth
Markup.OutlineWidth.help:
How far the legibility halo extends beyond the object, in pixels, when Outline is on.

1 to 2 is enough to separate the object from its background. Much more starts to read as a deliberate two-tone outline, which is a look rather than a legibility aid.

Text labels use half this for their halo, since glyph strokes are thinner than shape strokes and a wide halo would close up the counters inside letters like e and a.

Markup.Shadow.label: Shadow
Markup.Shadow.help:
Give new objects a drop shadow.

Off by default, for three reasons: Outline already does the legibility job that shadows do in other annotation tools, every shadowed object costs a second full draw, and the snip window may already have its own drop shadow - shadowed annotations on a shadowed snip is a lot of shadow.

It is a hard offset copy rather than a blurred one, which reads correctly at screenshot scale and costs almost nothing. Per object on the palette.

Markup.ShadowOffset.label: ShadowOffset
Markup.ShadowOffset.help:
How far down and to the right an object's drop shadow is displaced, in image pixels, when Shadow is on.

2 to 4 gives a shadow that reads as depth. Larger values start to look like a second, misaligned copy of the object, because this shadow is a hard offset rather than a blur - see Shadow.

Markup.ShadowAlpha.label: ShadowAlpha
Markup.ShadowAlpha.help:
Opacity of an object's drop shadow: 0 is invisible, 255 is solid black.

Around 100 to 130 reads as a shadow over most screenshots. Push it much higher and the offset copy competes with the object itself instead of sitting behind it.

This is the shadow on MARKUP OBJECTS. The snip window's own shadow is the separate ShadowAlpha in the SnipShadow section.

Markup.HighlightAlpha.label: HighlightAlpha
Markup.HighlightAlpha.help:
Opacity of a highlighter rectangle: 0 is invisible, 255 is solid.

The point of a highlighter is that you can still read what is underneath, so keep this low - roughly 70 to 110 behaves like a real marker pen. Above about 150 it stops highlighting text and starts covering it.

Highlighter objects are always filled and never get a halo, regardless of FillShapes and Outline.

Markup.ArrowHeadScale.label: ArrowHeadScale
Markup.ArrowHeadScale.help:
Arrow head size as a multiple of the arrow's stroke width, so heads stay in proportion when you change Thickness instead of needing to be retuned.

Around 3 to 4 looks like an arrow. Below 2 the head barely reads as one; above 5 it becomes a triangle with a short tail attached.

There is a floor of 8 pixels, so a 1px arrow still gets a head you can see.

Markup.Pixelate.label: Pixelate
Markup.Pixelate.help:
How the Blur tool hides what is underneath it.

Pixelate is the default and the better choice for redaction: it is cheaper, and a reader can SEE that something was deliberately hidden rather than wondering whether the image is just out of focus.

Either way the pixels are genuinely destroyed in the saved or copied image, not merely covered over - redaction is applied to the image before any rotation or flip, so there is no original underneath to recover.

Markup.BlurAmount.label: BlurAmount
Markup.BlurAmount.help:
Strength of the Blur tool: the image inside the rectangle is shrunk by this factor and blown back up, so the number is effectively the block size in pixels when Pixelate is on.

8 to 12 destroys ordinary body text. Small text on a high-DPI screenshot may need more - check the result at full size, because a value that looks safe at a glance can leave large headings readable.

Markup.HandleSize.label: HandleSize
Markup.HandleSize.help:
Size in pixels of the square grab handles on a selected markup object.

The clickable area is a little larger than the square you see, so a small handle is still easy to hit. Raise this if you work on a high-DPI display and the handles look like specks.

Handles are drawn into the on-screen image only. They can never reach a saved, copied or uploaded image.

Markup.HandleColor.label: HandleColor
Markup.HandleColor.help:
Color of the selection handles and the dashed selection boxes. Six hex digits, RRGGBB, no prefix.

It wants to be a hue you would never draw an annotation in, so that selection chrome is never mistaken for part of the markup. If you routinely annotate in blue, change this to something else.

Also used for the rubber-band rectangle when you Shift+drag to select several objects.

Markup.UndoDepth.label: UndoDepth
Markup.UndoDepth.help:
How many undo steps each snip keeps.

Undo stores a whole snapshot of the object list per step rather than a reversible command, which is what makes it impossible for undo to drift out of step with what is on screen. The objects are small records, so even a deep history costs very little - the exception is pasted images, which are shared between snapshots rather than copied.

The history belongs to the snip and dies with it; closing a snip discards it.

Markup.PaletteAutoShow.label: PaletteAutoShow
Markup.PaletteAutoShow.help:
Whether the tool palette appears automatically when you enter markup mode.

Turn it off if you know the single-letter tool keys and would rather not have a second window on screen; F3 still summons it when you want it.

The palette does not take focus when you click it, so the tool keys keep working while it is open and the snip stays the active window.

Markup.PaletteGap.label: PaletteGap
Markup.PaletteGap.help:
Gap in pixels between the snip and the tool palette when the palette is first placed.

It parks to the LEFT of the snip if there is room, flipping to the right if there is not, and clamps onto the monitor either way. Once you drag it somewhere, that position is remembered for the rest of the session and this setting no longer applies.

Markup.PathTurnTolerance.label: PathTurnTolerance
Markup.PathTurnTolerance.help:
How far the cursor must travel ACROSS the current segment, in pixels, before the Path Arrow tool commits a corner and starts a new segment at right angles.

This is the one Markup setting whose right value depends on you rather than on the image: too low and ordinary hand jitter spawns phantom elbows mid-drag, too high and a deliberate short jog gets swallowed. Somewhere around 10 to 20 suits most people; try moving it a few pixels at a time rather than in big jumps.

The same number decides what happens when you change direction almost immediately: a segment shorter than this is treated as you changing your mind, so the path turns on the spot instead of leaving a stub behind.

Measured in screen pixels during the drag, so on a high-DPI display it covers less of the image and may feel tighter than the number suggests. Values below 4 are ignored.

Markup.PathCornerRadius.label: PathCornerRadius
Markup.PathCornerRadius.help:
Radius in pixels of the rounded elbows on a Path Arrow. Rounding is applied when the path is drawn, not baked into it, so changing this restyles existing paths rather than reshaping them.

Setting this to 0 does NOT give you square corners: the stroke width is used as a floor, because a thick path with tight corners looks pinched against its own line weight. To get genuinely sharp elbows you would need a hairline Width as well.

The radius is also capped at half of the shorter of the two segments meeting at each corner, so a tight jog degrades to a sharp turn instead of overshooting into its neighbour. That means very short segments will look less rounded than the rest of the path, which is correct rather than a glitch.

Markup.PathMaxSegments.label: PathMaxSegments
Markup.PathMaxSegments.help:
Upper limit on how many segments one Path Arrow can have, so that a wild or shaky drag cannot produce a path with hundreds of corners in it.

On reaching the limit the tool stops committing new corners and simply keeps extending the segment you are on, so the drag carries on working rather than stopping dead.

The default is far more than a readable annotation needs - a path with more than about six turns is usually telling you the arrow should have started somewhere else. Raise it only if you genuinely draw long routed paths. Values below 2 are ignored.

Markup.LineDash.label: LineDash
Markup.LineDash.help: Dash pattern the Line tool starts with. Built-in names: solid, dash, dot, dashdot, dashdotdot. Any pattern you define in the [MarkupDashes] section can be named here too. An unrecognised name falls back to solid.

Markup.LineCapStart.label: LineCapStart
Markup.LineCapStart.help: End treatment at the start of a new Line. Built-in names: none, arrow, stealth, hollow, chevron, bar, dot, circle, square, diamond, plus anything defined in [MarkupCaps]. An unrecognised name falls back to none.

Markup.LineCapEnd.label: LineCapEnd
Markup.LineCapEnd.help: End treatment at the finish of a new Line. Same names as LineCapStart. Setting this to arrow is the only thing that distinguishes the Arrow tool from the Line tool.

Markup.ArrowDash.label: ArrowDash
Markup.ArrowDash.help: Dash pattern the Arrow tool starts with. Same names as LineDash.

Markup.ArrowCapStart.label: ArrowCapStart
Markup.ArrowCapStart.help: End treatment at the tail of a new Arrow. Same names as LineCapStart. Set this as well as ArrowCapEnd for a double-headed arrow.

Markup.ArrowCapEnd.label: ArrowCapEnd
Markup.ArrowCapEnd.help: Arrowhead at the point of a new Arrow. Same names as LineCapStart. This is the one people change most often, and it is what makes the Arrow tool an arrow.

Markup.PathDash.label: PathDash
Markup.PathDash.help: Dash pattern a new Path Arrow starts with. Same names as LineDash. Dashes follow the rounded elbows, so a dotted path reads well as a connector.

Markup.PathCapStart.label: PathCapStart
Markup.PathCapStart.help: End treatment at the start of a new Path Arrow. Same names as LineCapStart. The cap angle follows the first segment, so it turns with the elbow it sits on.

Markup.PathCapEnd.label: PathCapEnd
Markup.PathCapEnd.help: End treatment at the finish of a new Path Arrow. Same names as LineCapStart. The cap angle follows the last segment.

Markup.PenDash.label: PenDash
Markup.PenDash.help: Dash pattern a new freehand Pen stroke starts with. Same names as LineDash.

Markup.PenCapStart.label: PenCapStart
Markup.PenCapStart.help: End treatment at the start of a new Pen stroke. Same names as LineCapStart. A freehand stroke is never trimmed back, so the cap is drawn over the first point rather than replacing part of the line.

Markup.PenCapEnd.label: PenCapEnd
Markup.PenCapEnd.help: End treatment at the finish of a new Pen stroke. Same names as LineCapStart. Useful for sketching a hand-drawn arrow.

Markup.RectCorner.label: RectCorner
Markup.RectCorner.help: Corner radius in image pixels for new Rectangle and Highlighter objects. 0 gives square corners, which is how rectangles were drawn before this setting existed. The radius is capped at half the shorter side, so shrinking a shape turns it into a stadium instead of tying itself in knots.

Markup.CalloutCorner.label: CalloutCorner
Markup.CalloutCorner.help: Corner radius in image pixels for new Callout bubbles. -1 means auto, which keeps the original radius derived from the font size so existing callouts look unchanged. Any other value is an explicit radius, capped at half the shorter side.

Markup.CtrlClickSelect.label: CtrlClickSelect
Markup.CtrlClickSelect.help: Ctrl+click an annotation to select it without leaving the drawing tool you are using. Works on a snip that is not in a markup session too, which starts one. A Ctrl+click on bare image is ignored, so dragging a snip by its middle is unaffected. Set to 0 to disable.

Markup.StickyTool.label: StickyTool
Markup.StickyTool.help: After a Ctrl+click borrows the Select tool, remember the drawing tool that was in hand and give it back at the next click on bare image. A click with no drag still just deselects, so only a drag actually draws. Set to 0 and the Ctrl+click is a one-way trip to Select.
